French literature encompasses centuries of artistic innovation and intellectual refinement, from medieval romance to contemporary philosophy-informed fiction. The nineteenth century especially established France as the literary superpower of Europe—the crucible of realism, naturalism, and modernism. French writers have consistently shaped what literature can be: rigorous in style, ambitious in form, and philosophically unsparing in vision.

Medieval romance and troubadour poetry established French as a language of literary prestige, rivalling Latin and Italian in cultural authority. French became the language of courtly love and refined sensibility. The seventeenth century produced classical tragedy through playwrights like Corneille and Racine, and moral philosophy through Pascal and La Fontaine that defined rational elegance. French classical drama established rules and hierarchies that dominated European theatre for centuries.

Nineteenth-century realism made France the center of literary innovation. Balzac's social architecture mapped society comprehensively. Flaubert's stylistic precision made every word matter. Maupassant's technical mastery perfected the short story form. Naturalism emerged as an extension of realism. Émile Zola pushed mimesis toward scientific determinism, depicting working-class life with clinical intensity. His novels read like sociological documents transformed into art.

Symbolism and decadence, represented by poets like Baudelaire, Mallarmé, and Rimbaud, pioneered modernism by privileging suggestion, musicality, and the dissolution of rational meaning. These poets made linguistic experimentation and subjective vision primary values. Twentieth-century France remained intellectually dominant. Existentialism through Sartre and Camus, structuralism through Foucault and Barthes, and poststructuralism reshaped not only French literature but global literary theory and practice.

French novelists have consistently foregrounded style and formal innovation. The how of writing is as important as the what, establishing exigent standards for literary craft. This commitment to form as content distinguishes the French literary tradition. From Proust's psychological depth to the nouveau roman's formal experimentation, French literature has persistently asked what the novel is for and what forms it can take.
